problem: The trap says the projected area is 'the rectangle you see looking along the shaft'. Looking along the shaft axis you see the circular cross-section of the journal, not a rectangle. The L × D rectangle is seen in side view, looking perpendicular to the axis. A student would memorise the wrong picture of why πDL is wrong.
fix: Write: 'Hydrodynamic bearing pressure acts on L × D, the rectangle you see in side view, looking at right angles to the shaft axis — not on the curved surface πDL that you would see looking along the axis.'

problem: 'Some syllabi call S the bearing characteristic number' is misleading. The bearing characteristic number (also called the bearing modulus) is normally defined as μn/p alone, without the (r/c)² factor; S with the square is the Sommerfeld number. The sentence invites students to drop the square.
fix: Say: 'Some books call the group μn/p the bearing characteristic number or bearing modulus. The Sommerfeld number is that group multiplied by (r/c)². Keep the two names apart.'

problem: 'r/c between 500 and 1500' — the usual quoted band for machined bearings is r/c ≈ 500 to 1000 (c/r ≈ 0.001 to 0.002); 1500 is at the very loose end and is not typical.
fix: Say 'r/c typically lies between 500 and 1000 for a machined bearing (c/r = 0.001 to 0.002)', and keep the r/c = 500 arithmetic that follows.

problem: Eccentricity and eccentricity ratio are used from Section 3 onward without a definition, but the symbol and its link to film thickness are needed to follow 'the journal rides higher'.
fix: Add one line at first use: 'Eccentricity e is the offset of the journal centre from the bush centre; the eccentricity ratio is ε = e/c, and the minimum film thickness is h₀ = c(1 − ε). High S means small ε and a thick film.'

problem: 'every length cancels inside the group' is not accurate: L, D and the r/c lengths do not cancel among themselves; they pair with W (through p = W/LD) to make the whole expression dimensionless.
fix: Say: 'μn is a pressure (Pa), so μn × LD/W is (pressure × area)/force, a pure number; S stays dimensionless whatever units you use, as long as you are consistent.'
